items.summary:
US stocks closed mixed on November 18 as investors digested Nvidia's results ahead of Anthropic's IPO pricing, while weighing the hawkish tone in Federal Reserve meeting minutes. The Nasdaq Composite finished modestly higher, gaining 101.50 points or 0.39% to close at 24,429.89, and the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index closed slightly lower after outperforming the broader market this year. Conversely, the S&P 500 reversed its earlier modest gains to settle negative, losing 18 points or 0.24% to end at 7,322.53, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell sharply by 566.39 points or 1.12%, closing at 50,193.03.

Nvidia's quarterly results released late on November 17 beat analyst expectations and forecast revenue above estimates; however, its shares still declined amid uncertainty surrounding co-founder Jensen Huang's sudden departure the previous week. Among other chipmakers, Intel and Micron lost ground while Advanced Micro Devices advanced. Analyst Ryan Detrick of Carson Group in Omaha noted that there have been many dark clouds over technology, chip stocks, and AI generally, but cautioned that the market is not falling apart entirely, as non-tech groups are performing well under the surface.

Anthropic's IPO was expected to price after the close on November 18. At the top of its US$70 to US$78 range, the offering would raise about US$64.4 billion and value the company at about US$1.4 trillion. In retail, Target jumped following an upbeat holiday outlook, while TJX surged after forecasting strong annual sales ahead of the holiday shopping season; Walmart's results were expected on November 19. Take-Two Interactive shares rose in anticipation of its Grand Theft Auto VI rollout.

Minutes from the Fed's October policy meeting showed the central bank remained focused on inflation risks and recognized the need for further rate hikes if the economy progressed as expected, with a few policymakers arguing the case for a 50-basis-point hike should incoming inflation data prove unfavorable. Consumer and producer price data released after the meeting indicated hotter-than-expected price growth. Fed governor Christopher Waller took a hawkish stance on November 18, urging greater aggressiveness in responding to inflation; this followed New York Fed president John Williams' comments on November 17, in which he favored tighter policy but saw no need for dramatic action. Financial markets were pricing in a near-certain probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike at the December meeting, according to CME's FedWatch tool. Detrick added that inflation remains stubbornly higher than anyone wants and predicted a likely 25-basis-point hike in December with additional hikes early next year as a real possibility.

Housing data released on November 18 showed mortgage rates climbing while building permits faltered and pending home sales dropped to a record low.
items.title: Wall Street ends mixed after Nvidia earnings and hawkish Fed minutes

items.summary:
Google introduces Gemini 4 Neon, a frontier-level model positioned for fast end-to-end task completion across software engineering, knowledge work and science. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, Neon ranks #3 overall with a score of 61, just behind larger, slower models; on the Vals Index it ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. It also ranks #2 on steerability — adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections — on the new Agent Arena Index, follows multi-step instructions well, and records its lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing.

Pricing is $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Neon rolls out today across the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, and Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app.

In enterprise work spanning spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio and video, Neon synthesizes inputs into structured deliverables within a single 1 million-token context window. On benchmarks it ranks #2 on the Vals Index (70.9%), reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench, tops most Surge AI categories across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling and complex constraint following, scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts, matches leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%), achieves #1 overall on Zapier's AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), and debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions.

On scientific and mathematical reasoning it is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%) and HLE-Diamond (71.3%). For production-ready code, Neon sustains performance through complex tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — standalone or as a fast Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity — cutting redundant file reads, sharing progress and handling context compaction reliably.

It ranks #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), scores 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% at its default high setting on FrontierCode 2.0; it leads SWE-sweep's mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and reaches a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity.

Neon offers four thinking levels that scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to each workload. At its default high level it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon; on the Vals index and Agent Arena at high it sits on the Pareto frontier with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest workloads while still costing 36%+ less per task than competitors at their highest setting.

For cyber defense, Neon produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench, achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). On WebExploitBench v1.2 it is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models. In vulnerability finding it achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%) costing roughly half as much per challenge; in exploitation validation via ExploitGym it uses half the tokens of Carbon; and in patching, reaching 70.7% on Collinear's CWE-bench v2 for a 3.4% uplift over Carbon.

On safety, Neon maintains Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on alignment and agentic behavior. It refuses just 1.98% of tasks on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 0% on Terminal-Bench-Science; in internal coding use its chain-of-thought and action misalignment monitor alert rates stayed below Carbon's baselines, with 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and shortcuts taken on just 2.45% of tasks — the lowest rate of any Gemini 4 model — alongside a 0.09% misaligned action rate on its agentic safety suite and a 99.2% pass rate on its agent honesty evaluation. On agentic behavior it reduces under-service by 43%–56% and overreach by 15%–35% across different effort levels, building on Carbon's baseline.

On Gray Swan's IPI benchmark for indirect prompt injection attacks planted in web pages, emails, documents or code, Neon resisted every attack at its highest thinking level with real-time safeguards, matching the 0.0% attack success rate reached only by other Gemini models.

In the Gemini app, Neon excels at frontier-level reasoning and fast responses: it writes clearly with well-structured responses in a natural tone, reads uploads like spreadsheets, PDFs and photos more precisely to produce reports and summaries, pulls details from Google apps such as Gmail and Docs, incorporates web sources for current research on topics like vendor pricing or complex market briefs, and runs tasks faster than larger models — analyzing billing statements to spot utility charge spikes or cross-checking receipts and documents to negotiate refunds.

Within the Gemini 4 family, Carbon tackles hardest long-horizon projects while Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution; Neon balances depth and efficiency for frontier-level reasoning in complex, high-frequency workflows. Access begins today via the paid-tier Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Android Studio (for paid Pro or Ultra subscribers), Google Antigravity, all Pro and Ultra subscribers in AI Studio, Gemini for business, and the model dropdown in the Gemini app; eligible Fairwind Program members will begin receiving access over the next few days.
items.title: Gemini 4 Neon: Pricing, Benchmarks and Safety of Google's New Frontier Model

items.summary: Anthropic set its initial public offering price at $83 per share, above the preliminary range of $70 to $78 established earlier in the week. The company is scheduled to begin trading under the ticker ANT with co-founder Dario Amodei and other founders ringing the opening bell on Nasdaq. At this pricing, Anthropic's total market value reaches approximately $1.26tn to $1.41tn across all shares counted, which would make it one of the largest initial public offerings in history—though still below SpaceX's June debut at a $1.77tn valuation under Elon Musk. Amodei and his six co-founders plan to sell roughly $260m worth of shares each through the offering; priced at the top of the range, their stakes would be valued above $18bn apiece. The prospectus lists datacenter computing power as Anthropic's primary expenditure, with purchase commitments and lease agreements exceeding $70bn over the next 12 months, more than $450bn by 2030, and a further $450bn due by 2045. As the first generative AI company to go public at this scale, Anthropic's performance may shape investor sentiment toward peers: OpenAI had planned an IPO later in the year but delayed it after CEO Sam Altman cited safety concerns, while Nvidia—whose chips power AI systems—recently saw its CEO Jensen Huang resign amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs. The debut arrives during a volatile period for both AI and markets, following last month's industry-wide slowdown marked by falling share prices at several companies over growing concern about the technology. The article notes these surrounding events but frames them as context rather than direct drivers of Anthropic's pricing decision.
items.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share for record AI debut on Nasdaq

items.summary: During Nvidia's quarterly earnings call on Tuesday, interim CEO Colette Kress announced that the company would not file its routine quarterly report—a 10-Q—with the SEC immediately. Instead, she said it planned to file 'in the coming weeks,' offering no reason for the delay at the time. The move drew widespread attention because Nvidia has typically filed its 10-Q on the same day it reports results; analyst Edward Dowd called it a 'red flag.' A 10-Q normally provides far more operational detail than an earnings press release, including sections disclosing legal proceedings and risk factors that could impair the business. UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri raised the delay during his callback after the call, and Nvidia told him the postponement related to whether additional information about its ongoing investigation into Huang would need to be disclosed in the filing. Arcuri noted this was 'related to the ongoing investigation and whether any additional risk factors would need to be added to the filing.' He still rates the stock a buy but lowered his price target from $240 to $220, while Nvidia shares trade around $150. On the same day as the earnings report, The Wall Street Journal reported that the SEC is investigating whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. This added scrutiny comes amid multiple federal probes into allegations that partners sold restricted Nvidia AI chips—Nvidia AI—to China. Investigations have come from Congressional committees and the Department of Justice regarding Megaspeed, a company run by Alice Huang, who had an affair with Jensen Huang and is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia is also conducting its own internal investigation after Huang admitted to the affair and allegations surfaced that he had affairs with other employees. The article notes Nvidia has not yet responded to requests for comment on the delay.
items.title: Nvidia delays routine SEC 10-Q filing amid investigations into Huang affair and China chip sales

items.summary: Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey argued that Nvidia's board is effectively giving China what it wanted by removing longtime CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, who led the company for 33 years before stepping down last week amid several controversies. Among those controversies was an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy who has been investigated for possibly smuggling Nvidia chips into China to circumvent U.S. export restrictions. Speaking onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Luckey said 'China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,' repeating a statement he had posted on X last week. He added that there is 'a reason it's knocking a trillion dollars off Nvidia's market cap' and argued China knows removing Huang makes America weaker. While Luckey disagrees with Huang's longstanding position that Nvidia should have more leeway to export chips to China, he also acknowledged that China benefits if its domestic chipmakers can challenge Nvidia's dominance. He explained that 'China doesn't want Nvidia to sell GPUs to Chinese companies,' noting there are Chinese companies wanting to buy Nvidia GPUs but facing no import permit because Beijing wants a domestically built processor industry rather than one dependent on the United States. Luckey pointed out that Nvidia itself has said China will not grant such permits, and cited interim CEO Colette Kress's statement during Tuesday's quarterly earnings call that Nvidia would no longer sell H200 chips in China at all. More than 200,000 people — including Elon Musk and the CEOs of Y Combinator, Databricks, Epic Games, Shopify, and Replit — have signed a petition calling for Huang's reinstatement. Despite founder Huang offering to return, Nvidia executives said during Tuesday's earnings call that the company has no plans to reappoint him.
items.title: Palmer Luckey wants ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reinstated after China benefits from his removal

items.summary: Coinbase reported that its AI-powered fraud-prevention systems blocked approximately $4.7 million (about 91%) of cryptocurrency transfers directed at scammers promoting a fake giveaway built around an AI-generated deepfake of Elon Musk during a Tesla livestream. The fraudulent stream appeared to broadcast the event, which drew more than 500,000 viewers, and displayed an AI-generated video of Musk alongside cryptocurrency wallet addresses and a QR code promising that any crypto sent would be doubled. According to Coinbase, hundreds of its customers attempted to send millions of dollars over roughly two hours, including many longtime users of the exchange. Unlike traditional theft involving compromised accounts or stolen credentials, victims here voluntarily initiated transfers after believing the livestream was genuine; they were logged in and confirmed transactions thinking it was a legitimate opportunity. This voluntary nature makes such scams harder to detect because standard fraud defenses are designed to flag activity customers did not authorize. Coinbase explained that its system uses machine learning models to analyze outgoing transfers in real time, identifying suspicious patterns tied to giveaway scams, brand impersonation, and newly created wallet addresses. When a transfer looks suspicious, an AI agent engages the customer in conversation, explaining scam characteristics and asking questions meant to help them recognize fraud; responses are assigned confidence scores so additional safeguards can be triggered when needed. Coinbase stated that this entire detection and intervention process operated automatically without human involvement. Notably, the company said its agent had never encountered this specific campaign before—deepfake giveaways tied to a live product launch were not in its training—but recognized the underlying techniques: promises to multiply cryptocurrency, time pressure linked to a live event, and irreversible transfers. BleepingComputer contacted Coinbase asking how many transfers reached the scammers and how much crypto was ultimately stolen but had not yet received a response at press time. Musk and his companies have long been popular targets for scams, with fraudsters previously hijacking verified Twitter accounts, sending fake giveaway invitations by email, flooding TikTok with fraudulent promotions, using deepfake videos to promote fraudulent investment platforms, and running one campaign involving compromised verified Twitter accounts that stole more than $580,000 in cryptocurrency within a single week. To avoid such scams, users are advised to independently verify crypto promotions through official websites and social media accounts rather than trusting livestreams or QR codes shown in videos.
items.title: Coinbase Blocks $4.7 Million in Transfers to Elon Musk Deepfake Scam

items.summary:
Over the past decade, MIT researchers have developed aerial microrobots with bumblebee-like speed, agility, and durability for tasks such as precision agriculture or search-and-rescue. Previously these featherweight robots could not carry navigation electronics, forcing them to remain connected to a motion-capture system in the lab. The team has now designed a flapping-wing microrobot with onboard sensors and computation that can follow a complex trajectory and land precisely on a sunflower outside the lab's motion capture environment. Although still tethered to an offboard power source during this demonstration, it highlights potential future uses for aerial microrobots in precision agriculture. Flying microrobots could weave through fields of almond trees or blueberry bushes to pollinate delicate blossoms in regions where natural pollinator populations have been decimated by habitat loss, and they could hover near plants without causing damage while monitoring crop health and spotting pests before they become widespread.

To enable onboard sensing and computation, the researchers developed a method to expand the artificial muscles that power the robot's wings. They carefully tuned the radius and length of the soft actuators, increasing their size by 50 percent while boosting the robot's net lift forces by 46 percent. This tuning allowed them to achieve a lift-to-weight ratio of 1.9, giving the robot more than enough lift force to carry an onboard electronics package weighing only 244 milligrams.

The tiny electronics package contains the sensors and microcontroller needed for onboard sensing and computation. It incorporates an inertial measurement unit to estimate attitude, an optical flow sensor to estimate lateral flight speed and position, and a time-of-flight sensor to measure height. Without the precision of an attached motion capture system, however, the robot does not know its absolute position, causing it to drift off course.

To overcome this challenge, the team designed a sensing algorithm that calculates the robot's orientation, angular velocity, and position extremely quickly by simplifying calculations to reduce computational cost. They found that estimating position continuously at a faster rate yielded higher performance than a more accurate but slower estimation. The researchers integrated the sensors and computing components into a tiny electronics package attached to a fiberglass substrate so it would not be thrown off by vibrations of the robot.

They tested the aerial microrobot's capabilities through flight demonstrations, including hovering at different heights and following point-to-point trajectories. The robot maneuvered quickly and precisely with positional errors of only a few centimeters. They also demonstrated potential for artificial pollination by using a joystick to send high-level position setpoints, guiding the vehicle around several plants before carefully landing on a sunflower.

The researchers analyzed the vehicle's power expenditures and found that the electronics consume about 6 percent of total power, with the rest fueling the robot's artificial muscles and wings. They identified ways to further reduce power consumption from the electronics, which would allow for the addition of more components such as a camera enabling object recognition.

The researchers are now working toward two goals: putting a camera onboard for autonomous object recognition and obstacle avoidance; and integrating power electronics and batteries onto the tiny robot, which would enable untethered flight in an outdoor environment. This research was funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), U.S. Office of Naval Research, U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and a Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

Kevin Chen, associate professor in MIT's Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-corresponding author of a paper on the robot, said: "This is quite difficult to do, even if you do have a motion-capture system." He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Yi-Hsuan (Nemo) Hsiao, Quang Phuc Kieu, and Zhongtao Guan; co-corresponding authors Jonathan P. How, Ford Professor of Aeronautics and Astronautics and principal investigator in LIDS and the Aerospace Controls Laboratory at MIT; Elizabeth Farrell Helbling, an assistant professor at Cornell University; and others at MIT.

The research appears today in Science Robotics.
items.title: MIT develops sensory and compute autonomous flapping-wing microrobot for precision agriculture

items.summary:
Minutes from the October Federal Reserve interest-rate-setting meeting, released on Nov 18 after a three-week lag, showed that almost all participants believed further rate hikes would be necessary to combat persistently high inflation. According to nearly every policymaker's baseline outlook for inflation and the labour market, additional hikes 'would likely be appropriate' to bring prices under control.

The Federal Reserve held rates steady at its previous late-October meeting even as chairman Kevin Warsh said inflation remained 'too high.' The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates within a target range of 3.75% to 4%, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, following its first rate hike in three years at the September meeting.

Two voting members, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, dissented in favour of an immediate 25-basis-point hike. Ten of the committee's 12 voting members called for rates to be held steady; these participants cited the need to assess the durability of AI-related investment demand, the evolution of financing conditions, the transmission of the September rate increase to the economy, or geopolitical developments.

The Fed maintains a dual mandate of keeping inflation at its long-term 2% target while ensuring maximum employment. The US unemployment rate has remained relatively steady over the past year despite seesawing job growth, attributed to demographic changes and lower immigration. PCE price index inflation—the Fed's preferred gauge—hit 3.6% in September, far above the central bank's target.

Inflation had been on a downward trajectory since its pandemic peak but reignited over the past year, driven by President Donald Trump's tariff policies and an energy price spike linked to his war on Iran. Massive infrastructure investments supporting the AI buildout have also contributed to higher prices. At the October meeting, participants 'acknowledged that inflation remained elevated,' with most remarking that inflation pressures were broad-based—indicating they saw increases spreading beyond soaring energy prices into other sectors.

Those who dissented from the majority's decision to hold rates said they viewed inflation as 'too high' and saw few signs of it abating. They judged that the current policy stance was not sufficiently restrictive, with a few warning that further delay risked allowing high inflation to become entrenched or necessitating a larger and more disruptive tightening later.

Speaking on CNBC before the minutes were released, Fed governor Chris Waller said he was 'very, very concerned' about inflation and now saw the need for a 50-basis-point hike at the December meeting. He added that the Fed may need to go beyond this prescribed hike to meaningfully fight inflation. Fed governor Michael Barr also spoke of the need for further rate hikes.

The article notes these are reported statements from individual officials, not official committee decisions; no specific vote tally is given for Waller's or Barr's positions.
items.title: Near-unanimous Fed view of further rate hikes amid elevated US inflation

items.summary:
RadixArk has released DaisyRose-27B, its first model, built on the Qwen3.8-27B architecture and trained via reinforcement learning using their open-source framework Miles. The training ran for 18 days across 144 H200 GPUs on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, drawing from about 1,200 curated tasks. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%, and scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B on every benchmark tested, with gains also reported across reasoning, instruction-following, and coding benchmarks. The model retains Qwen3.8-27B's architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window; scores use the higher of BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark, which differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated.

Three components enabled this release: task design, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes. Tasks were built in partnership with Eigent AI from a large pool spanning machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields; about 1,200 made the final set after selection on three criteria—each targeting a mistake the original model makes (with difficulty adjusted until solve rate fell within a useful range), requiring several interdependent steps across long jobs with up to 1.5 hours per attempt in a sandbox involving more than 100 tool calls and more than 256K output tokens, and rewarding actually solving the problem after manual review of every task alongside model attempts.

Training ran on Miles in fully asynchronous mode: while 128 H200s run inference on agent tasks, 16 additional GPUs run the trainer (built on Megatron) learning from trajectories; updated models go out to the 128 agent GPUs after each step. The release achieved 57% lower training cost versus the open-source trainer—37% of peak compute went into useful work via model FLOPs utilization, compared with 16% for Megatron on comparable runs—with even larger gains reported on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash. The release also ran about 2× faster end to end, at approximately 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs versus about 8,300 for the open-source trainer; it trained steadily over six weeks totaling 63,000 GPU-hours.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox built on AgentENV. Between mid-September and mid-November, the service ran about 944,000 sandboxes with up to 1,566 running concurrently; it grew from one machine to as many as 12, shipped ten upgrades nearly all while training was running, achieved 99% success in sandbox creation across nine weeks (exceeding 99.95% since late October), and kept cloud infrastructure costs about 80% lower than popular cloud providers by letting each sandbox's memory allocation scale with usage.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0, recommended to be served with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding; the model thinks before answering by default, returning reasoning in reasoning_content and its final answer in content via an OpenAI Python client example on port 30,000. RadixArk thanks Eigent AI for training data, the Qwen team for Qwen3.8-27B, and communities behind Miles, SGLang, slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.
items.title: RadixArk Releases DaisyRose-27B: RL-Tuned Agent Model on Qwen3.8-27B with Major Efficiency Gains

items.summary: ZDNET reports that Apple is launching an improved Health app with the release of iOS 27.3, expected next month (December). Rather than only recording and displaying health statistics, the new app will use Apple Intelligence to analyze data from various sources and offer advice on improving health and fitness. However, AI-powered features require a compatible iPhone that supports Apple Intelligence; other features remain available to all users. The first feature provides insights based on aggregated health data: for example, it may suggest walking at a nearby park if insufficient exercise is detected, surface articles or videos about sleep when rest appears inadequate, or flag possible conditions from lab and test results — all viewable via an Insights screen. A new 'Health Age' feature compares physical health to chronological age using stats such as resting heart rate, sleep, heart rate variability (HRV), cholesterol, and A1C, potentially revealing areas of concern. Movement Evaluations lets the app assess flexibility, strength, balance, VO2 max, and overall movement; users perform a routine while an iPhone 'watches' them via camera with an Apple Watch, delivering real-time audio and visual feedback through on-device AI that does not record, store, or share video. The updated app can also correlate test results with data from the iPhone and Apple Watch for a broader health picture, supported by an optional partnership between Apple and Quest Diagnostics offering US customers a $119 bloodwork panel covering more than 50 biomarkers to screen for various conditions. Finally, workout videos normally requiring an Apple Fitness+ subscription will be included directly in the Health app's Insights section as strength-training content spanning key body areas.
items.title: Apple's iOS 27.3 Health app adds AI-driven insights and fitness features in December

items.summary: The article reports that AI models can solve difficult mathematical problems, including some open research questions from the Mathematical Olympiads. Because agents are prone to hallucination, their proofs must be checked; this is done with proof assistants such as Lean (favored by many mathematicians), HOL Light (used at AWS to verify high-performance cryptographic code, including post-quantum cryptography), and Isabelle (used at AWS to verify the Nitro Isolation Engine). The authors focus on Isabelle. To let an AI agent communicate with a proof assistant they use the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which is supported by leading agents. They announce three publicly available tools in the AutoCorrode verification suite: I/Q, enabling an agent to hand over control of a live Isabelle session; I/R, enabling an agent to develop proofs while the user keeps working without taking control; and Isabelle Assistant, powered by I/Q, providing a chat window that can observe and modify a user's session. Proofs are written in a formal logical language designed for both computer checking and human readability.
items.title: AI-Generated Mathematical Proofs Verified by Isabelle at AWS

items.summary: IONNA, a DC charging operator backed by several major OEMs, has opened its largest DC charging site to date at a new 'Rechargery' in Westminster, California. The facility features 22 bays of peak 400kW capacity: 12 CCS connectors and 10 NACS ports, allowing nearly any EV to charge (though no Chademo is supported). In addition to the chargers, the site offers indoor and outdoor lounge space, restrooms, an in-store convenience area using Amazon's 'just walk out' technology with ceiling cameras that track items taken and charge a card accordingly, trash cans, window wipers, and nearby amenities including an In N Out and a taco shop across the street. The Westminster location is described as IONNA's flagship station and its first closer to the population center of the LA metro area; other chargers exist in South OC and the Inland Empire, with more opening soon. The site address is 6260 Westminster Blvd, just off the 405 freeway. Charging at the new location runs at a promotional rate of $0.20/kWh for the first weeks, after which IONNA's standard rate of $0.39/kWh applies. Alongside the opening, IONNA announced that Tesla EVs can now use its network with Plug & Charge functionality (technically 'Autocharge'), enabling drivers to link their car and credit card via the Presto charging app ahead of time and simply plug in without tapping or swiping; this mirrors the experience Tesla owners have on Superchargers. The feature is rolled out across IONNA's entire network starting today, building on existing Autocharge support for BMW, GM, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Rivian, Ford, Porsche, and Volvo EVs. Stellantis EVs (Jeep, Dodge, Ram, Fiat) are listed as 'coming soon,' with Plug & Charge expected in December; IONNA states it now supports Autocharge for about two thirds of the EVs on American roads. The Westminster opening also capped off a cross-country roadtrip by IONNA personnel who departed from various parts of the country and convened at the new site, where over 20 EVs joined and drove over 40,000 combined miles; during the trip, teams charged at approximately 30% of the company's charging sites. The article notes that no Chademo support is available and that an AC-only Tesla Roadster cannot charge there.
items.title: IONNA Opens Largest Westminster DC Charging Site and Enables Tesla Plug & Charge

items.summary: A publicly traded artificial intelligence lab is arriving as the market for its boom enters an inflection point. Anthropic is expected to price its initial public offering later in the day, ahead of first trading on the Nasdaq under ticker ANT; it plans to sell 825 million shares at between $70 and $78. This debut comes just over 24 hours after Nvidia's earnings call, during a two-week stretch that saw CEO Jensen Huang ousted amid multiple affairs including one with a Chinese spy, a blue-wave midterm election tied to data center backlash, signs of slowing data center construction, and concern about AI's promise versus its enormous expenditures. Morningstar senior equity analyst Travis Miller said the IPO and Nvidia's strong showing could pump confidence back up after utilities had endured a rough couple of weeks; he noted that "utilities and investors are watching the landscape very closely because data center growth is a key part of the investment story for utilities in the coming years," and asked whether utilities can continue to meet expectations if the bubble deflates. Anthropic does not build its own data centers but contracts many, which rely heavily on fossil fuels; the company's prospectus mentions clean energy sources such as solar, wind, battery storage, nuclear, and geothermal only briefly, warning they "may not be available in the quantities or on the timelines we require, or may be available only at higher cost." Construction in progress for Anthropic totaled $877 million by end of September 2026, against purchase commitments and lease agreements aggregating approximately $895.4 billion, substantially all related to compute and infrastructure. The filing set a rough timeline: about $69.8 billion over the coming year, roughly $447.5 billion expected by 2030, with most of the remainder between 2031 and 2045; as capacity grows, Anthropic said associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased. The company dedicated much of its risk assessment to power-supply variability and regulatory uncertainty, writing that "electric grid infrastructure in the United States and other countries was not designed to accommodate the rapid increase in demand associated with AI development." It is primarily turning to natural gas for new compute; the Financial Times reported a $3.4 billion deal for more gas-fired generators from Texas-based OnePWR Solutions for 1.7 GW of generator power. An analysis by the nonprofit Better Data Center Project found Anthropic has made no direct commitments to renewable energy in the U.S., that its data centers are mostly sited where grids rely heavily on coal and gas, and that "currently contracted data centers in the U.S. will be overwhelmingly powered by fossil fuels in the near term." Lacking clean-energy commitments, post-IPO grid demand may mean more fossil infrastructure; when behind-the-meter sources are used, researchers said gas turbines are often less efficient and more polluting. Estimating on-site gas plus likely grid power plants for added load, they concluded about 87% of Anthropic's power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028. Nvidia's Tuesday evening call followed a tumultuous two weeks; interim CEO Colette Kress and board director Harvey Jones sought to reassure jittery investors that the company was shaking off its Huang ouster, with Jones putting rumors of his possible return to rest. Kress raised next-year sales guidance from 70% to 75% expected growth and said commitments to partners would not change; she opened her remarks with "our momentum is real" and closed with "we've got this." She also addressed the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus, a massive facility SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, is developing in southern Ohio with Anthropic's competitor OpenAI as tenant. The project relies on an unusually tangled financing arrangement; SoftBank recently canceled some advance payments for power equipment across its U.S. data center projects, raising doubts. Kress said Nvidia has $105 billion in credit support for land, power, and shell capacity at the campus, with plans on track and capacity expected online in phases beginning calendar 2028. Investor confidence in AI buildout pace had been waning before Anthropic's launch; two recent analyses point to a downturn in data center development. Market intelligence firm Cleanview found new construction fell 28% in the last quarter versus the previous quarter, the first such drop since early last year, though it remains twice last year's pace, so its persistence is unclear. The Financial Times analyzed changes in total market capitalization over the year for energy, manufacturing, and mining companies tied to AI infrastructure buildout and found a sharp drop in later months of 2026: Caterpillar, which supplies gas generators to data centers, fell 44% since June 30; Bloom Energy rose 300% in the first six months of 2026 but then dropped more than 30% between June and November; and advanced nuclear company Oklo dropped nearly 50% despite an agreement with Meta. Miller warned that "any pullback in demand could cause a hit."
items.title: Anthropic's Nasdaq IPO lands amid a shaky AI-infrastructure market

items.summary: On Wednesday, Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share, above the targeted range of $70 to $78 reported by Bloomberg News. The sale is described as one of the largest stock-market IPOs on record and the first by a major frontier artificial intelligence model developer, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified because the information isn't public. Anthropic initially planned to sell 825 million shares, though the size of the offering has since increased. The pricing followed a roadshow that attracted demand several times the number of shares offered, Reuters previously reported, despite questions about the company's outlook and its ability to sustain rapid growth as competition in the AI industry intensifies. Anthropic's sale is the second mega-IPO this year focused on AI, following June's SpaceX offering, even as chipmakers and cloud companies central to the business have come under pressure due to valuation concerns, mounting AI infrastructure costs, and Jensen Huang's sudden resignation as CEO of Nvidia. The company's annualized revenue run rate reached $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion from September 30, according to its IPO filing. Anthropic reported that it had 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in annual revenue on a trailing 12-month basis as of September 30, compared with more than 1,500 at the end of last year. Sustaining growth is becoming expensive: Anthropic spent nearly $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, nearly four times the amount spent a year earlier, and incurred an additional $5 billion in computing costs in the third quarter. Revenue rose 47 per cent in the third quarter to $16.96 billion, while the company reported an operating loss of $567 million compared with operating income of $974 million in the second quarter; net loss fell to $23.3 billion from $66.3 billion a quarter earlier, including non-operating items related to bonds convertible into its shares. Anthropic has committed to nearly $900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google. The prospectus warned that some of these providers depend on third-party financing and credit support to acquire chips and build capacity, noting that if such financing becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered. CEO Dario Amodei has called for the industry to slow the pace of developing and releasing increasingly powerful models, warning that advances in AI could outstrip society's ability to manage the risks. Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley serving as lead underwriters alongside a 22-bank syndicate; both banks also led SpaceX's IPO earlier this year. Anthropic declined to comment.
items.title: Anthropic prices blockbuster AI IPO at $83 a share

items.summary:
Anthropic is set to make its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, trading under the ticker ANT. The company's first funding round was a $124 million Series A raised in 2021, led by co-founder Jaan Tallinn well ahead of Claude's commercial launch, according to CNBC. Tallinn's current holdings remain undisclosed, but with Anthropic expected to debut at about $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis, his payout could rise into the tens of billions—though the final figure depends on how much later fundraising reduced his stake and whether he sold any shares.

Tallinn is known for warning that AI may threaten humanity; in a 2020 conversation with CNBC, he estimated a one-in-six risk of not surviving the century, drawing on Toby Ord's work. He co-founded the Cambridge Centre for the Study of Existential Risk and the Future of Life Institute, which issued the 2023 "Pause Giant AI Experiments" letter.

Anthropic's earliest backers came from charitable networks concerned about existential danger posed by AI. Tallinn and CEO Dario Amodei moved in overlapping effective altruism circles; he saw backing a safety-focused AI company as among the most effective ways to mitigate that risk.

The company has signaled it expects to price its IPO at or above the top of its $70 to $78 range, which would value Anthropic at about $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis—up from the $965 billion valuation in its most recent private funding round.

Many AI safety advocates object to the listing, fearing that commercial success and a broader shareholder base will deprioritize safety work. To address governance concerns, Anthropic's co-founders alone make up Founder, which controls 50.1% of voting power. The company is also structured as a public benefit corporation with a stated purpose of responsible AI development for the long-term benefit of humanity.

Tallinn declined to be interviewed by CNBC.
items.title: Anthropic co-founder Jaan Tallinn could earn billions in Nasdaq debut despite existential-risk warnings

items.summary: On Wednesday (Nov 18), investors absorbed a strong third-quarter report from chipmaker Nvidia while preparing for the long-awaited public offering of AI startup Anthropic, yet stocks fell across the board amid ongoing industry uncertainty. The technology sector faces questions over whether large AI investments will ever pay off, and has been rocked by claims that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who may have funneled restricted chips to Beijing. Alongside reports of affairs with Nvidia employees, these allegations led to Huang's resignation as chief executive last week, raising doubts about the prospects for one of the world's largest companies. In its highly anticipated earnings release on Tuesday, Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue that doubled to more than US$115 billion (US$115,000,000,000), generating a net profit of US$65.3 billion (US$65,300,000,000). The firm also raised its forecast for next year's revenue to 75 per cent (%75) growth. However, investors noted that the United States moved to tighten restrictions on Chinese access to chips, and Huang has agreed to meet US lawmakers on Dec 1 to answer questions about national security concerns. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said: "For Nvidia, strong earnings have bought management time." He added that for the broader AI trade, the results reinforce confidence in infrastructure demand, but the next leg of the rally may depend increasingly on which companies can turn that demand into sustainable profits. Interim CEO Colette Kress described the situation as "business as usual" following the loss of Huang, a pivotal figure in the eye-watering growth of the artificial intelligence industry. The US markets were unforgiving for Nvidia, whose shares fell by 2.9 per cent (%) (2.9) by close in New York, continuing weeks of heavy losses and matching a slump across two of the three main US indexes on Wednesday, with the Nasdaq the only one to close in the green. European bourses also slipped into the red at close of play, as did most markets in Asia. Analysts suggested many investors were likely reducing holdings in other stocks to free up funds for Anthropic shares. Peter Cardillo from Spartan Capital Securities said: "Investors are preparing for a blowout IPO tomorrow from Anthropic." He hoped it might begin to alleviate some of the worries the market is undergoing. The five-year-old startup was going public Thursday in an IPO that could raise US$65 billion (US$65,000,000,000) or more, giving investors a first chance to bet directly on a stand-alone AI giant and testing how long the sector's spending boom can last. David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation, noted that the issue was over six times subscribed, with plenty of excitement ahead of the first public offering of a pure frontier lab at the forefront of AI development. Anthropic is widely seen as the leader for AI products, while Nvidia has been dubbed the "central bank" of the industry for its investments in start-ups and backstops on loans. On currency markets, the dollar extended recent gains against major rivals on expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month and possibly again early next year. That could slow economic growth but would raise returns on US government bonds, considered one of the safest investments available. On Wednesday, minutes from the Fed's last meeting in October showed that "almost all" policymakers expected further hikes to be necessary, with Governor Chris Waller telling CNBC he could back a 50 (50) basis-point increase.
items.title: Stocks fall despite Nvidia's blockbuster earnings as Anthropic IPO looms and Fed rate-hike bets build

items.summary: A live financial blog reports that the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) is set to open lower following AI company Anthropic's initial public offering, which was priced above market expectations. The ASX200 futures were down 0.6% to 8,809 points at around 7:15am AEDT, with the Australian dollar falling 0.3% to 67.12 US cents. Across global markets, Wall Street showed mixed results—Dow Jones -1.0%, S&P 500 -0.2%, Nasdaq Composite +0.5%—while European indices declined more sharply: FTSE -1.3%, DAX -1.2%, and Eurostoxx600 -1.0%. Spot gold fell 3.3% to $US3,724/ounce, Brent Crude dropped 1.7% to $US91.59/barrel (oil trading under $US92), iron ore was down 1.2% at $US88.05/tonne, and Bitcoin fell 2.9% to $US62,479. US 10-year bonds stood at 5.07%, with Australian yields at 5.09%. Anthropic priced its IPO at $US83 ($124) per share on the Nasdaq under ticker ANT, above expectations of $US70 and $US78 a share, in one of the largest stock-market IPOs on record. The offering could raise up to $US64.4 billion and put it at a valuation exceeding $US1 trillion, with an estimated 825 million shares sold plus an additional private placement of $US26 billion among strategic investors. Founded in 2021 by specialists who previously worked at OpenAI—including Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei—Anthropic competes with ChatGPT and Gemini through its Claude assistant, generating revenue from companies that integrate the tool into their products and operations. Large shareholders Amazon and Alphabet (parent company of Google) own around a third of the company; existing investor Zoom Communications invested in 2023 under $US51 million in undisclosed 'strategic investments,' part of a partnership allowing Zoom to use Claude AI, which Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei described as bringing 'robust, steerable AI' to more people. Separately, Domain's forecast predicts Australia's housing market downturn will drag on into next year across every major city; Sydney is expected to lead a national price recovery with house prices falling 10 per cent by June 2027 before stabilising in the second half of that year, and median prices rising from $1.6 million to $1.7 million over the 12 months to December 2027—driven by high borrowing costs and weak buyer confidence, with national falls projected between 10 and 13 per cent across major capital cities by mid-2027. Nvidia shares dipped about -3% despite strong September quarter earnings that more than doubled revenue; since its October 6 record high, the stock has fallen 36%, largely tied to co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation following revelations of extramarital affairs including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang and two with employees. Analyst estimates for Nvidia's next fiscal year adjusted net income have climbed to $US393 billion from $US380 billion, while the average price target dipped to $US251.74 from $US265.70 on Monday; shares closed at $US151 per share.
items.title: ASX to open lower as Anthropic IPO priced at $US83 a share

items.summary: This is a news brief previewing an upcoming episode rather than reporting completed events. The segment centers on Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who was scheduled to accompany the U.S. president to the APEC summit in Shenzhen but has been removed from that itinerary following revelations about his relationship with a Chinese national and allegations involving a Singapore client's backdoor circumvention of sanctions on Nvidia's H200 chips. The hosts intend to examine the fallout from these disclosures, including any subsequent tightening of U.S. chip export restrictions to China; internal infighting within the Trump administration over how to respond; and whether Huang's removal represents a high point in Silicon Valley's effort to dominate artificial intelligence markets quickly. They also raise open questions about consequences for rivals such as OpenAI and Anthropic ahead of their anticipated stock market debuts, and whether the United States will instead double down on export controls and impose its will where it can. The hosts note that Shenzhen is home to major domestic tech champions as well as Chinese headquarters of U.S. companies like Walmart, and they frame a broader reflection on how global anxieties have shifted from nuclear proliferation to artificial intelligence over time. No figures are reported in the item beyond these qualitative assertions.
items.title: Nvidia scandal and US-China AI competition ahead of APEC summit

items.summary: The US House Committee on Energy and Commerce launched an oversight inquiry into Nvidia's handling of allegations involving its former chief executive, Jensen Huang. In a letter dated Wednesday, Committee Chairman Brett Guthrie requested a briefing from Nvidia's Interim Chief Executive Officer Colette Kress no later than Dec. 2. The committee said it was examining allegations that Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence, as well as reports that a senior Nvidia official attempted to intervene in a federal government investigation involving the company. The inquiry comes amid growing scrutiny of Nvidia's internal security controls, export compliance procedures and potential exposure of sensitive American semiconductor technology to China. The committee emphasized that its investigation falls within its congressional oversight responsibilities on interstate and foreign commerce, consumer protection and the implementation of federal laws. Huang announced Nov. 12 that he was stepping down as CEO; Nvidia later named Kress, its chief financial officer, interim CEO. US and Singaporean authorities previously investigated Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's customers, for allegations that it helped Chinese companies circumvent US restrictions on advanced chip exports. Guthrie wrote in the letter: "Understanding what happened, how it happened, and how to move forward are critical to mitigating the impacts of this ongoing situation, ensure national and economic security, and ensure that the U.S. continues to be a global leader in the AI stack."
items.title: US House Committee Demands Nvidia Briefing Over Alleged Chinese Spy Links and Chip Export Investigation

items.summary: Anthropic, the maker of Claude, is expected to begin trading on Nasdaq on Thursday at a price range of $70-$78 per share, which would value the company at up to $1.4 trillion; final pricing was anticipated Wednesday night. Model-based estimates suggest substantial employee wealth could result from the listing: Hill, a San Francisco-based private-share marketplace, estimated that 598 non-founder employees could hold at least $100 million in equity each after the IPO, while Sacra estimated around 2,800 current and former employees could have at least $1 million in pretax vested equity at a valuation of $1.35 trillion; Reuters noted both estimates are model-based, rely on publicly available information, and could not be independently verified. Anthropic disclosed that employees holding stock options had accumulated $119 billion in paper gains as of September 30, based on a weighted average exercise price of $2.91 per share, with around $73 billion of these gains vested and exercisable immediately. Early employees stand to gain the most because their options carried lower exercise prices: those granted through 2023 and still outstanding at year-end averaged just 52 cents per share. Benson observed that early employees who started in very junior roles should have a better financial outcome than someone joining in a senior role right before the IPO. Non-founder employees may sell up to 10% of their holdings on the first trading day, followed by another 35% after fiscal 2026 earnings. Founded in 2021, Anthropic expanded its workforce to approximately 5,300 employees by September 30 from around 940 at the end of 2024, with stock-based compensation playing a significant role; a May 2024 job advertisement for an administrative business partner offered a salary of $140,000-$190,000 while describing equity as 'a major component of the total compensation.' In 2024, Anthropic granted stock options at an average exercise price of $1.30 per share; CFO Krishna Rao received 14 million such options in 2024 at that same $1.30 exercise price each, which could carry approximately $1 billion in gross intrinsic value before exercise costs and taxes. Marcelo Ballve, head of research at Sacra, noted this pattern is common at venture-backed companies like SpaceX, though Anthropic may reserve such grants primarily for recruiting top talent following its IPO.
items.title: Anthropic's Nasdaq IPO Could Turn Thousands of Employees Into Millionaires

items.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller called Wednesday for more aggressive action against inflation, saying the central bank must be “a little more aggressive in our rate hikes to try to get inflation down,” per an interview with CNBC. He cited recent three-month data implying an annualised inflation rate of about 3.5%, well above the Fed’s 2% target. Waller said the Federal Reserve could either raise rates by 50 basis points in December or deliver two quarter-point increases across December and January, but argued the second path would only work if officials clearly signalled that another hike would follow in January; without such a “credible signal,” financial markets would not reflect the full impact of the planned increases. He had first raised the possibility of a half-point increase on November 10, warning that a larger move might be needed to preserve inflation-fighting credibility, and his comments came shortly before data showed core consumer prices rose 0.3% from the previous month, reaching the level he identified as strengthening the case for a bigger hike. Waller’s stance is more hawkish than several other policymakers; New York Fed President John Williams pushed back against an outsized move on Tuesday while acknowledging the central bank still had work to do to return inflation to its 2% target. Quoting Williams: “I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action.” He added that the Fed’s approach of taking time to evaluate incoming data had worked well, at an Axios event in New York. Interest-rate futures indicate investors expect quarter-point increases in December and January, followed by another hike by April.
items.title: Fed Governor Waller pushes for a larger December rate hike amid persistent inflation

items.summary:
In her first all-hands meeting as interim CEO, Nvidia's Colette Kress opened by addressing compensation. Speaking to nearly 49,000 employees on Wednesday a week after founder Jensen Huang resigned, she said staff should expect pay raises and more equity in December, months ahead of the usual schedule. She framed the message around taking care of each employee so they would not worry about their comp.

Compensation was the top question among roughly 700 submitted by employees before the meeting; the next most common request was for greater board transparency. That concern is understandable given that Huang resigned on November 12 amid allegations of extramarital affairs, reportedly including two with Nvidia employees and one with Alice Huang (no relation), a businesswoman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. China denied any espionage operation, and Nvidia has hired Wachtell Lipton to probe whether his conduct compromised national security or company secrets. Huang is due to testify before Congress on December 1.

Huang's quarterly town halls were normally a major draw inside the company with details rarely leaking; Wednesday's meeting broke both patterns. Board chair Harvey Jones, opening Tuesday's earnings call, said the board "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Kress has backed that line, stating the board determined it would not reinstate him and that focus is now on growing the business for employees, customers and shareholders. Outside the company, thousands of employees reportedly lobbied for Huang's reinstatement; an online petition backed by Elon Musk, Garry Tan and Tim Sweeney drew close to 200,000 supporters, and President Donald Trump said he "would not mind" a return.

Huang left the door open in a Tuesday post on X, admitting to "serious mistakes" in his personal life, promising to cooperate with the board's investigation, and saying he would be "honored" to return if the board felt it was best for shareholders, employees, the company and America. The board instead hired search firm Heidrick & Struggles to look at internal and external candidates. On prediction market Kalshi, Arm CEO Rene Haas leads at 25%, followed by Nvidia's Ian Buck at 17% and Huang at 9%.

Retention is now the top priority for Kress. Investors fear a brain drain; many senior engineers are already wealthy and some stay for the mission Huang drove rather than the paycheck. On the earnings call, a Bank of America Securities analyst asked about retention, to which Kress said stabilising the employee ranks was "probably the most important thing" leadership is thinking about. She added that they would take care of employees during this transition so work could continue in the current environment.

The numbers give her room to spend: third-quarter revenue more than doubled to $115.8 billion, data centre revenue rose 110% to $107.6 billion, profit hit a record $65.3 billion, and Nvidia expects $130 billion in the fourth quarter. Shares rose about 5% on Wednesday. Even so, the company is still worth roughly $2 trillion less than at its October peak.

Cofounder Chris Malachowsky joined Kress for a short Q&A to take the culture question. He said he, Huang and the other cofounders thought putting values on posters was "nonsense," because culture shows up in how people behave and work together. Malachowsky concluded with "We're going to be fine," which the article frames as Nvidia's way of making sure its people stay long enough to see if that holds true.
items.title: Nvidia's interim CEO promises early pay raises amid Jensen Huang ouster and board rejection of his return

items.summary: A 64-year-old retired man from Antop Hill in Mumbai was defrauded of Rs9.35 lakh after downloading a malicious application titled 'LIFE CERTIFICATE UPDATE'. The fraud exploited the annual life certificate submission process that pensioners must complete to continue receiving their pensions. On November 8 at around 1.15 pm, the victim came across a bank advertisement on Facebook related to pension services and clicked on the link provided in it. He then downloaded an application named 'LIFE CERTIFICATE UPDATE' and was prompted to enter his pension-related details. The application subsequently sought his ATM card details, including his PIN. Shortly afterwards, he received a WhatsApp message from an unknown mobile number containing an APK file bearing the same name, along with a call instructing him to download it. After installing the APK, the victim started receiving OTPs on his phone and was instructed by the caller to type certain numbers into his device. Unaware of being targeted, he followed the instructions, allegedly allowing fraudsters remote access to his mobile screen. Multiple unauthorised transactions then occurred, debiting Rs9.35 lakh from his bank account. The victim contacted the national cybercrime helpline 1930 on November 11 and approached the Antop Hill police station with a formal complaint. Police registered a case against unidentified persons under relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and the Information Technology Act, examining mobile numbers used by the accused, transaction records, and beneficiary bank account details to trace the money trail. The report attributes these events as alleged actions by fraudsters; police have urged pensioners to avoid downloading APK files from unknown sources and never share ATM PINs, OTPs, or banking details with strangers.
items.title: Mumbai Pensioner Loses ₹9.35 Lakh to Fake Life Certificate App Fraud
